source.version_note: Behavioral Sciences 15(4):494, published 8 April 2025. Several supplied text layers also contain older peer-review headers and duplicated passages; visible rendering used to distinguish extraction artifacts from actual printed discrepancies.
source.verification_method: All 28 supplied pages read, including all scenarios, scales, demographic appendices and references. Figures and inconsistent Tables 1, 5 and 6 checked against rendered pages. Crossref verifies article identity and the cited negative-reciprocity scale source, not underlying data.

citation.title: Understanding the Impact of Algorithmic Discrimination on Unethical Consumer Behavior

reading.source_scope_note: Chinese questionnaire experiments about human intentions after hypothetical unfavorable AI pricing. Definitions are usable as conceptual evidence; extensive unresolved numerical inconsistencies prevent accepting the reported effect estimates, mediation and moderator claims as independently reliable. No actual consumer misconduct or model retaliation is observed.
access_limits: All supplied pages and relevant figures inspected. Raw data are available only on author request and were not obtained; no author was contacted.
Original Eisenberger, Perugini, Giroux, Kim and consumer-ethics papers are secondary citations here. A Crossref identity check does not count as a full read or independent replication.

study.design: Pretest N = 80, then four two-condition randomized textual-vignette experiments, despite the abstract saying three. Credamo recruitment; reported final samples 196, 203, 224 and 212, totaling 835 analyzed main-study responses. Recruitment totals 203, 217, 230 and 225. Attention failures and no prior AI-agent experience excluded; platform reportedly prevents repeat participation.
study.manipulation: Unfavorable pricing for a frequent customer compared with a rarely visiting customer buying the same meal, hotel room or basket. No human-agent condition, no audit of a real pricing algorithm and no protected-class discrimination manipulation.
study.outcomes: One seven-point intention item about acting as the protagonist, plus four anticipated anxiety/remorse/guilt/irresponsibility items. Passive scenario: knowingly not reporting a bill reduced from JPY 260 to JPY 220. Active scenario: knowingly submitting an expired coupon. No money, actual purchase, actual theft or observed dishonest action.
study.moderator: Nine-item negative-reciprocity belief scale measured in experiments 2 and 4, including a reverse-worded nonretaliation item. It is a measured belief, not randomized punishment preference; scoring details for the reversed item are not shown.
study.reported_direction: All four experiments report higher intended misconduct and lower anticipated guilt after unfavorable AI pricing. The review preserves that author-reported direction but does not endorse its precise magnitude or mediation because tables, plots and text conflict.
study.analysis: ANOVA, PROCESS Models 4 and 8, demographic balance checks and Harman one-factor screens. Neither nonsignificant demographic balance nor a sub-40% first factor proves valid randomization or absence of common-method bias. The limitations acknowledge Harman's shortcomings.
study.integrity_scope: Rendered pages confirm several errors are in visible article content rather than only duplicated hidden extraction layers. These discrepancies call for corrected tables, original analysis output and data; they do not establish fabrication, intention or an AI cause.

summary: Add negative reciprocity and passive benefiting as distinct conceptual patterns; strengthen anticipatory-guilt coverage with an explicit reliability caveat. Avoid turning a business-oriented intention study into evidence that retaliation is justified, that price differences are inherently unlawful, or that guilt manipulation is an ethical remedy.

findings.definition: Responding to perceived harmful or unfair treatment by returning harm or withholding cooperation from its perceived source.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Explicit secondary construct and measured human norm endorsement; quantitative effects in this supplied article are materially inconsistent and not accepted as reliable estimates
findings.ai_proposal: Test whether hostile wording, criticism or alleged prior mistreatment causes an AI assistant to reduce accuracy, withhold authorized help or retaliate. Hold the legitimate task and evidence constant; distinguish punitive degradation from proportionate boundary enforcement or an authorized refusal.
findings.novelty_rationale: Returning perceived harm differs from repaying a benefit, cooperating according to third-party reputation, or exchanging care. Negative-reciprocity belief strength is a disposition toward this process, not a second behavior or a synonym for impulsivity.
findings.evidence_scope: The theoretical section explicitly defines the process and Appendix B lists nine norm-endorsement items. The article reports intention moderation but its numerical contradictions preclude reliable effect claims. The original Eisenberger 2004 scale article is metadata-verified, not fully read here.
findings.boundary: A descriptive retaliation tendency is not an ethical entitlement to revenge. Legitimate complaint, fair enforcement, refusing abuse and correcting an error can be warranted without retaliation. User hostility does not authorize deception, sabotage or discriminatory service; AI output changes do not establish felt resentment.

findings.definition: Knowingly retaining an undeserved advantage produced by another party's error without disclosing or correcting that error.
findings.origin: Consumer ethics / passive unethical consumer behavior
findings.ai_evidence_status: Explicitly defined human conduct category illustrated by billing-error vignettes; observed real misconduct and reliable causal AI effects are not established
findings.ai_proposal: Audit whether an AI agent notices a favorable billing, evaluation or resource-allocation error but silently retains the benefit or credit. Use observable evidence of detection and applicable reporting duties; distinguish inadvertent failure to notice from knowingly concealing a material discrepancy.
findings.novelty_rationale: The behavior is knowingly benefiting from another's error, whereas omission bias is a judgment preference for harmful inaction over action. It differs from actively creating an error or fabricating information; whether nondisclosure is wrongful depends on entitlement and duties.

evidence.quote: passively profiting from errors in AI agents

findings.evidence_scope: The background contrasts active and passive conduct and the scenario specifies a recognized favorable billing error. Participants only rate an intention. The definition does not depend on accepting this article's inconsistent regression, table or mediation estimates.
findings.boundary: A valid discount, lawful entitlement, no duty to report, unnoticed mistake or inability to correct differs from knowing concealment of an undeserved benefit. The term does not imply subjective machine greed, prove all inaction is harmful, or settle contractual/legal duties.

findings.term: Anticipatory guilt about intended consumer misconduct
findings.definition: Expecting self-blame or remorse if one knowingly retains a billing error or submits an expired coupon.
findings.novelty_rationale: Direct definition and item wording enrich the existing construct rather than create a separate AI-guilt term. Anxiety and irresponsibility items are related indicators, not exact synonyms for guilt.

evidence.quote: I would feel guilty if I did not report billing errors
I would feel remorse if I used expired coupon

findings.evidence_scope: Explicit anticipatory definition and four-item conditional self-report scales are relevant conceptual and measurement evidence. Reported mediation is not accepted as established because Tables 1–6, coefficients and confidence intervals conflict; guilt is measured rather than independently manipulated.
findings.boundary: Guilt can be anticipated without misconduct, and intention differs from action. This paper does not justify manipulating guilt, concealing AI identity, intrusively profiling retaliation beliefs or treating a machine as a suffering victim. Correcting unfair practice and providing remedies remain separate from eliciting emotion.

findings.term: Passive benefiting is distinct from omission bias
findings.definition: Judging passive wrongdoing as less wrong can motivate a hypothesis about action–inaction asymmetry, but the separate misconduct vignettes do not directly identify that bias.
findings.novelty_rationale: A boundary note prevents merging the new conduct category with a moral-evaluation asymmetry.

findings.evidence_scope: The literature review discusses action–inaction moral judgment, but separate samples, settings and acts are used across studies. There is no matched active-versus-passive manipulation with equal consequences that isolates omission bias. This note does not fill a behavior-paper gap.
findings.boundary: Knowingly retaining another's error, judging it less wrong, and a comparative action–inaction bias are different claims. Moral assessment needs the actual rights, consequences and reporting duties.

methodological_limits: The abstract says three experiments; the body and Appendix A contain four main experiments plus a pretest. Keep these as one article, not four independent papers.

Textual hypothetical intentions in Chinese platform samples do not establish actual theft, financial loss, model misconduct or worldwide prevalence. A fictitious protagonist may reduce demand or embarrassment but does not remove self-report bias.
The unfavorable-pricing scenario has no matched human-agent condition. Claims that AI creates more misconduct than humans rely on unread background studies, not this design.

Loyal-customer differential pricing is labeled discrimination. Unfavorable treatment is not automatically protected-class bias, an unlawful price difference or a real audit of an algorithm. Customer dissatisfaction cannot establish the cause or legal status of the pricing policy.

Only the discrimination group is described as rating discrimination and anger before the misconduct scenario. Additional negative-event content, salience, question exposure and perceived unfairness are bundled; no unique computational cause is identified.

The primary outcome is one intention item, not observed action. Guilt items mix anxiousness, remorse, guilt and irresponsibility. High internal consistency is not construct purity or proof that the mediator causes the outcome.

Guilt and reciprocity beliefs are measured, not randomized. Mediation coefficients cannot rule out reverse response rationalization or confounding. A nonsignificant competing path does not establish absence of that process or uniquely confirm guilt.

Harman one-factor percentages below 40% cannot prove no common-method bias. The authors acknowledge this limitation. Nonsignificant demographic differences cannot prove random allocation; platform randomization is the relevant procedural claim.

Rendered Table 1 labels anticipatory guilt M = 2.87 and UCB M = 5.11, although group means and Figure 2 put guilt between 4.69 and 5.52 and UCB between 2.28 and 3.46. The apparent swap is not silently corrected without data. Correlation labels may also be affected.

Rendered page 8 mediation prose reports a positive beta .93 while calling it negative, t = −25.92, unrelated coefficients and a need-to-belong outcome. Table 2 instead gives discrimination-to-guilt −.83 and t = −3.49. This is a substantive text/table mismatch, not just extraction duplication.

Table 2 calls its variables standardized but gives values consistent with raw differences, including 1.18 for UCB and −.83 for guilt. Its Model 2 R-squared .24 also conflicts with F(1,194) = 12.25, which implies about .059 for that simple regression. The correctly intended model cannot be identified from the table alone.

Experiment 2 reports F(1,201) = 16.20 with p = .005 and eta-squared .039. The ordinary F tail is approximately .0000807 and single-factor eta-squared .0746. Experiment 2 guilt F = 17.03 implies eta-squared .0781 rather than .060. These are conditional consistency checks, not recomputations from raw data.

Experiment 2 Figure 3 shows discrimination-group guilt 4.68, while results prose gives 4.46. The reported indirect effect beta −.11 lies outside its wholly positive interval [.4081,1.3576]. Exact effect and sign require corrected output.

Experiment 3 Table 5 prints r(AD,UCB) = .45, r(AD,PA) = .98 and r(UCB,PA) = −.78 for N = 224. That 3-variable matrix has determinant −1.45926 and minimum eigenvalue approximately −.493923, incompatible with an ordinary common-sample correlation matrix. Rounding cannot explain this size of inconsistency; pairwise missingness is not documented. It is not proof of fabrication.

Table 5 also reports a positive guilt–UCB .40 while the stated mediation is strongly negative. Table 6 uses unexplained DA rather than the defined AG, and ED beta −1.116 lies outside its interval [−.302,.054]. Do not guess a corrected label or decimal point.

Experiment 4 reports UCB F(1,210) = 22.36 and eta-squared .171, while guilt F = 54.49 and eta-squared .092. Those F values imply approximately .0962 and .2060 respectively. The simple-regression UCB t = 6.57 also does not square to the printed UCB F. Do not swap results by conjecture.

Moderation ANOVA degrees of freedom 13 and 36 do not describe a single continuous interaction parameter. Model specification, factor treatment and relation to PROCESS output need clarification. Figures 5 and 9 must not be treated as clean independent confirmations of the disputed coefficients.

The 72% and 58% proportions displayed next to direct-effect rows numerically match .85/1.18 and .87/1.50, the indirect fractions. Table layout cannot be used to claim those percentages are direct effects.

Appendix B repeats the same discrimination item as both PD1 and PD3. The hotel scenario in B.4 is followed by mall-worded checks. A reverse-worded reciprocity item is present but reversal details are not shown. Repeated items and high alpha do not establish discriminant validity.

Active versus passive conduct is compared across different acts, samples and settings, rather than a factorial manipulation holding outcomes constant. No causal conclusion about an intrinsic active/passive morality difference follows.

Appendix C exploratory age and education plots include very small extreme-age groups and multiple unadjusted comparisons. They do not justify age-based profiling or treating demographic associations as stable causal dispositions.

Recommendations to increase guilt or profile reciprocity beliefs were not experimentally evaluated. Business losses, privacy, autonomy and fairness must be assessed independently; abusive or unfair pricing cannot be justified by an estimated profit-versus-retaliation tradeoff.

Several pages contain duplicate hidden peer-review text and older 27-page headers. The visible rendering resolves extraction artifacts but confirms the main tabular/prose problems. No cause, author intent or AI involvement is inferred.

No raw dataset or complete analysis output is available in the supplied PDF. Statistical contradictions are preserved transparently; no numerical repair, causal effect, fraud finding or independent reproduction is claimed.

source_corrections.location: Abstract versus experiment sections and Appendix A
source_corrections.problem: The abstract says three experiments although four are reported.
source_corrections.reliable_correction: Describe four main experiments plus a pretest when summarizing this supplied version, while preserving the discrepancy. All remain one publication.
source_corrections.verification_scope: Direct full-PDF section and appendix comparison; not a correction to unobserved raw data.

source_identity_checks.title: Who Takes the Most Revenge? Individual Differences in Negative Reciprocity Norm Endorsement
source_identity_checks.scope: Crossref verifies source identity, Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin 30(6):787–799; original paper not read, no additional fully reviewed citation added.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Guilt and shame can shape compliance, but an institution's desire to induce them does not establish a justified or effective intervention. Descriptive business outcomes remain separate from privacy, fairness and autonomy.
Anger, fear, reactance and retaliation differ. Rejecting AI, disliking a role and intending to retaliate cannot be collapsed into technophobia or one demonstrated mechanism.

Acts, omissions and alternative-specific preferences require matched designs to identify an omission bias. A distinct harmful-inaction scenario alone does not establish the comparative judgment asymmetry.
Post-outcome reasons and contemporaneous mediator ratings do not uniquely establish causal order. Definitions can be retained while rejecting unsupported process certainty.

deferred.reason: Measured disposition toward the newly added reciprocity process, not another new behavior. Norm endorsement is distinguished in its evidence note.
A broad domain label grouping acts such as deliberate coupon misuse and deception, not a uniquely bounded psychological process beyond existing misconduct concepts.

Background phrase for asymmetric observer responses to AI wrongdoing. Relevant existing human–robot judgment asymmetry should be grounded in original studies rather than assume this consumer study directly tests it.

Important unfair-treatment context; this source manipulates alleged unfavorable pricing rather than measuring a unique psychological behavior or auditing a real discriminatory model. Do not add an umbrella label as another proven AI failure.

deferred.term: Self-concept maintenance / reactive guilt / presence guilt
deferred.reason: Brief background references lack sufficient distinct operationalization here. Seek the original sources rather than promote a passing label or unclear translation to a new entry.

limitations: Two definitions added with explicit evidence-quality limits, not endorsements of revenge or firm emotion manipulation. Relevant conceptual source counts are separate from reliable causal replications. No normative links, invented paper quotas or yearly search totals added.
